description: A 3D Moon south pole explorer that compares landing sites by sunlight, Earth visibility, and comms windows using LOLA terrain data.
summary: Centauri Lunar Atlas is a browser-based 3D Moon explorer for the Lunar Landing Site Navigator challenge. It compares historic landing sites and candidate regions by how local terrain affects sunlight and direct visibility to Earth. NASA LOLA elevation, LROC imagery and JPL Horizons positions power a terrain-horizon model over a shared 30-day window. Users can inspect sunlight availability, longest sampled darkness and Earth visibility, compare up to three sites, then fly over or walk across the surface. The goal is to make the relationship between lunar geography, solar power and communications understandable and explorable. Built solo with JavaScript and three.js, it brings public NASA datasets into an accessible interactive tool. Results are preliminary, resolution-dependent estimates for education and exploration, not certified mission-design predictions.
details:
THE PROBLEM

Lunar site selection is a terrain problem: nearby polar ridges and crater floors can have very different illumination and direct-to-Earth visibility. Lunar Atlas makes those differences explorable using real NASA elevation and imagery.

WHAT IT DOES

Explore a full 3D Moon; search lunar features; visit Apollo, Luna, Chang’e, Surveyor and CLPS locations; and inspect selected south-pole terrain targets. Compare up to three sites over the same November 14–December 14, 2026 UTC window. The visibility panel reports sunlight fraction, longest sampled dark stretch, and Earth visibility, with qualitative solar-availability categories. Free-flight and Walk modes bring users down to the surface, including jumping under lunar gravity (1.62 m/s²). Historical candidate-region proxies and illustrative future CLPS regions are distinguished from confirmed landings.

HOW IT WORKS

Plain JavaScript and three.js render a cube-sphere quadtree with 33 × 33 vertex tiles, level-of-detail terrain and seam skirts. Global LOLA LDEM_16 elevation is supplemented by selected LROC NAC Apollo-site terrain and 5 m NASA Goddard PGDA south-polar grids. LROC WAC imagery supplies the global texture. JPL Horizons Sun/Earth positions are sampled every six hours. The model evaluates body centers against terrain horizons and compares all sites over identical dates. Python notebooks and scripts prepare the source rasters and ephemerides for browser use.

WHY IT MATTERS

The project connects orbital-scale context, site comparisons, and an eye-level view of the same terrain. Students and space enthusiasts can investigate why latitude alone cannot determine solar availability or Earth visibility. For example, the documented window gives Connecting ridge approximately 78% sunlight and a longest dark stretch of 6.8 days; these estimates make the need for storage tangible.

LIMITATIONS

This is an exploratory visualization, not a flight-qualified landing, power, or communications analysis. Terrain resolution varies; six-hour sampling can miss transitions; partial solar disks, sub-grid obstacles, and energy-balance calculations are not modeled. Solar verdicts are qualitative. Synthetic micro-relief is visual detail, not measured fine-scale terrain. Historical Artemis candidate-region proxies are not current touchdown assignments; planned mission pins indicate regions rather than exact landing coordinates.

AUTHORSHIP AND AI DISCLOSURE

Built solo by Weston Rosch during NASA Space Apps Mountain View. I was the one who had the ideas for literally everything; I selected and processed the datasets and made the design decisions, ran testing, and constantly iterated. Grok Bot, ChatGPT/Codex, and Devin assisted with code authoring, debugging, technical research, and documentation/editorial review in order to make a solo project like this possible. Original datasets remain attributed to their sources. Location markers use three.js geometry and CSS. Historical photographs and third-party mission illustrations are separately credited.
